IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Hughes v. Hughes,

2011 BCSC 1569

Date: 20111118

Docket:
S104238

Between:

Eva Hughes also known as Maria Hughes

[
1
]

The plaintiff brings this action against her
parents for a series of wrongs allegedly done to her, beginning almost 20 years
ago. The defendants apply to strike out the claim as being vexatious and an
abuse of process. In the alternative, they seek an order that the plaintiff
post security for costs. The plaintiff brings her own application to strike out
the defence because the defendants failed to appear at an examination for
discovery.

[
2
]

The plaintiff, who is now 37, alleges in her
statement of claim that:

•

In 1992, when she was pregnant at the age of 17,
her parents forced her to have an abortion, which she says has resulted in
“severe and continuous psychological injuries.”

•

In or sometime after 1995, her father induced her
to give him access to an investment account she owned and then withdrew all of
the funds from that account without her knowledge.

•

In 2000, her father caused the corporate
defendant, of which he is the principal, to register a fraudulent mortgage
against property she owned and she was required to commence petition
proceedings to remove it.

The defendants deny all of these
allegations and for the purpose of these applications it is neither necessary
nor appropriate to refer to the allegations or the responses to them in any
further detail.

[
3
]

The defendants’ application is brought pursuant
to Rule 9-5 (1) and (2), which read:

9-5 (1) At any stage of a proceeding, the
court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a
pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a) it discloses
no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be,

(b) it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c) it may
prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of the proceeding, or

(d) it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court may pronounce judgment or
order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the
application to be paid as special costs.

(2) No evidence
is admissible on an application under subrule (1) (a).

[
4
]

On an application to strike pleadings under what
is now rule 9-5 (1) (formerly rule 19 (24)), the court does not engage in a
detailed consideration of the merits of the action. For purposes of the
application, the court assumes the facts alleged by the plaintiff are true and
considers only “whether [...] the plaintiff can present a question fit to be
tried.”
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,

1999 CanLII 5860
(BCSC) at para.
37
.

[
5
]

In regard to what is now Rule 9-5(1)(a) the
Supreme Court of Canada said in
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2
S.C.R. 959 at p. 980:

...assuming
that the facts as stated in the statement of claim can be proved, is it
"plain and obvious" that the plaintiff's statement of claim discloses
no reasonable cause of action? As in England, if there is a chance that the
plaintiff might succeed, then the plaintiff should not be "driven from the
judgment seat". Neither the length and complexity of the issues, the
novelty of the cause of action, nor the potential for the defendant to present
a strong defence should prevent the plaintiff from proceeding with his or her
case. Only if the action is certain to fail because it contains a radical
defect ranking with the others listed in Rule 19(24) of the British Columbia
Rules
of Court
should the relevant portions of a plaintiff's statement of claim
be struck out under Rule 19(24)(a).

[
6
]

One paragraph of the statement of claim meets
that test and counsel for the plaintiff concedes that portion of the pleadings
cannot stand. In paragraph 11, the plaintiff claims that in allegedly coercing
her into having an abortion, the defendants violated her rights under the

Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
. This is clearly a dispute between
private citizens to which the charter has no application and paragraph 11 must
be struck, along with the paragraph I C of the prayer for relief, which also
refers to the Charter.

[
7
]

The balance of the statement of claim makes
allegations that essentially amount to battery, breach of trust and fraud, all
of which are well-recognized causes of action. As said above, this action is
not yet at a stage where the court is to consider whether there is sufficient,
or any, evidence to support those causes of action or to weigh conflicting
evidence.

[
8
]

The defendants say the plaintiff’s claim is
bound to fail because it is clearly barred by the
Limitation Act,
R.S.B.C.
1996, c. 266. This action was commenced in June 2010 and alleges wrongs
committed as far back as 1992. The relevant sections of the
Limitation Act

would appear to be:

3(2) After the
expiration of 2 years after the date on which the right to do so arose a person
may not bring any of the following actions:

(a) subject to subsection (4) (k), for damages in respect of injury to
person or property, including economic loss arising from the injury, whether
based on contract, tort or statutory duty;...

(3) After the
expiration of 10 years after the date on which the right to do so arose a
person may not bring any of the following actions:

...

(b) against a trustee in respect of any fraud or fraudulent breach of
trust to which the trustee was party or privy;...

(5) Any other action not specifically provided for in
this Act or any other Act may not be brought after the expiration of 6 years
after the date on which the right to do so arose.

[
9
]

In
Fuoco Estate v. British Columbia,

2001
BCCA 325
, the Court of Appeal said at paragraph 15:

Counsel have
been unable to direct us to any cases in which Rule 19(24)(a), standing alone,
has been used to resolve a limitation issue. That may be because statements of
claim do not raise limitation issues, as is the case here. The statutory
limitations is a defence pleading. It is an issue that does not arise until it
is pleaded in defence.

[
10
]

That passage was cited by Leask J. in
Rain
Coast Water Corp. v. British Columbia,

2008 BCSC 1182
, at paragraph
26
. The
court in
Rain Coast
also identified a potential question of whether the
limitation period had been postponed. The postponement provisions are contained
in ss. 6 and 7 of the
Limitation Act
.

[
11
]

Without attempting to foreclose any other
postponement argument the plaintiff might make, her allegation that she
suffered from severe and continuous psychological illness would appear to make
s 7(2) the most relevant postponement provision. That section reads:

s. 7(2) If, at the time the right to bring an action
arises, a person is under a disability, the running of time with respect to a
limitation period set by this Act is postponed so long as that person is under
a disability.

[
12
]

It will ultimately be for the plaintiff to prove
any postponement of the limitation period. That is a factual inquiry that must
take place at trial (perhaps a summary trial) and cannot be dealt with on
application to strike pleadings.

[
13
]

The defendants also say that the entire
statement of claim should be struck pursuant to Rule 9-5(1) (b) and/or (d) as
being vexatious and an abuse of process. They say this action is brought purely
for the purpose of causing them emotional and financial hardship in their
retirement years, as evidenced by correspondence in which the plaintiff
threatens to “break” and “crush” them.

[
14
]

Vexatious actions include those brought for an
improper purpose, such as harassment or oppression of the other parties:
Ebrahim
v. Ebrahim
,
2002 BCSC 466
, at paragraph
15
. Actions brought for an improper
purpose may also be characterized as abuse of process, as will actions that
involve a deception of the court or the process of the court not being fairly
and honestly used:
Babavic v. Babowech
, 1993 Carswell 2950, at paragraph
18.

[
15
]

Those considerations most commonly arise where
there is an attempt to re-litigate matters that have already been decided or
that could have been raised in previous proceedings. That was the case in both
Ebrahim

and
Babavic
, but is not the case here. In
Citizens for Foreign Aid
Reform
, Romilly J. said that a pleading is vexatious if “it does not go to
establishing the plaintiff’s cause of action or does not advance any claim
known in law.” Romilly J. continued at paragraph 48:

[48]

In
the case at bar, the defendants contend that paragraphs 9 and 10 of the
Statement of Claim are unnecessary, scandalous and vexatious and that they will
prejudice, embarrass and delay the fair trial of this proceeding. There can be
no doubt that both paragraphs are "scandalous" in their offensive
imputations against the character of the defendants. However, an allegation
that is scandalous will not be struck, even if written maliciously or
mala
fides
, if it is relevant to the proceedings. The question before this court
then, is do the impugned pleadings constitute allegations of fact relevant to
and necessary for the purpose of furthering the plaintiff's cause of action?

[
16
]

This case clearly arises out of an unfortunate
situation in which the plaintiff has come to have an extremely high level of
animosity and anger toward her parents. But all of her allegations, however
extreme or shocking they may be, however much distress and embarrassment they
may cause the defendants, are relevant to the plaintiff’s efforts to prove her
claim under known causes of action. It is not for me to comment at this stage
on the merit of those claims or the likelihood of success.

[
17
]

The defendants have not demonstrated grounds for
striking pleadings under Rule 9-5(1) and their application must be dismissed,
except as it relates to the allegation of a breach of charter rights.

[
18
]

The defendants seek, in the alternative, an
order that the plaintiff post security for costs. They say she has no history
of steady employment and would not likely be able to pay costs if the action is
dismissed. The plaintiff says in an affidavit that she is employed as a
pre-school teacher, but gives no particulars of that employment.

[
19
]

The law governing security for costs was
summarized by Goepel J. in
Bronson v. Hewitt
,
2007 BCSC 1751
. Although
the court has inherent jurisdiction to order an individual resident in the
jurisdiction to post security for costs, that jurisdiction should be exercised
cautiously, sparingly and only under very special or egregious circumstances.

[41]

...For good reason, individual
and corporate plaintiffs have always been treated differently. Absent special
circumstances, corporate shareholders are entitled to avail themselves of the
protection of a limited liability company to avoid personal exposure for costs:

P.G. Restaurant Ltd.  v. Northern Interior Regional Health Board et al.
,

2006 BCSC 1680
. An order for security for costs prevents the principals of a
corporate plaintiff from hiding behind the corporate veil and, as noted by
McGarry V.C. in
Pearson
, protects "the community against
litigious abuses by artificial persons manipulated by natural persons."

[42]

With individuals, the fundamental concern has always been access to
the courts. Access to justice is as important today as it was in 1885 when Lord
Bowen declared in
Cowell
that "the general rule is that
poverty is no bar to a litigant". Individuals, no matter how poor, have
always been granted access to our courts regardless of their ability to pay a
successful defendant's costs. Only in egregious circumstances have individuals
been ordered to post security for costs.

[
20
]

Examples of such special or egregious
circumstances include situations where the plaintiff is or has been a party in
multiple other actions (
Louie v. Louie
,
[1998] B.C.J. No. 2097
), or
where the plaintiff has been unable to produce any evidence in support of his
claim many years after commencing the action (
Rotvold v. Rocky Mountain
Diesel Ltd
.,
[1997] B.C.J. No. 1758
). No comparable special circumstances
have been shown to exist here and the evidence as to the plaintiff’s alleged
impecuniosity is entirely speculative.

[
21
]

The application for security for costs must
therefore be dismissed.

[
22
]

The plaintiff seeks an order striking out the
statement of defence because the defendants failed to attend an examination for
discovery. At the time, the defendants were requesting production of certain
documents. Those documents had not been received and, until shortly before the
scheduled examination for discovery, counsel for the defendants understood that
the former counsel for the plaintiff was still assembling them.

[
23
]

This is not an appropriate case for an order
striking out pleadings. At the close of oral argument, I made an order for
production of the requested documents and I am assuming that, once they are
produced, there will be no difficulty arranging the necessary examinations for
discovery.

[
24
]

This matter is set for trial on January 3, 2012
and I seriously doubt whether it can be ready to proceed. The parties are
required to schedule a Trial Management Conference pursuant to Rule 12-2 and I
direct that they schedule one as soon as possible if they have not already done
so. At that Trial Management Conference, the parties should be in a position to
address the issue of whether the matter is ready for trial, along with any
remaining discovery issues.

[
25
]

Costs of these applications will be in the
cause.

“Smith J.”
